Comprehension of Passages.intro: Comprehension tests whether you can read carefully, find information, understand what the writer means and express the same idea in other words. In JAMB English, the questions are short, but every answer must be supported by the text, so accuracy matters more than speed of reading.

blocks.x: 1. What JAMB tests in comprehension
Questions fall into a few predictable types. Learn to recognise the type first, because each type has its own way of finding the answer.

head: Question type
What it asks
How to find the answer
rows: What is the passage mostly about?
Read the first and last sentences of each paragraph; the main idea covers the whole passage, not one detail.
What does the passage say about X?
Find the keyword in the passage and read the sentence around it.
Use clues in the text; the answer is not stated directly but is clearly suggested.
What does a word mean here?
Use the sentence around the word; replace the word with each option.
Look at word choice: praise, criticism, humour, concern, neutrality.
Which option says the same thing?
Keep the meaning; do not add, remove or reverse an idea.

blocks.x: 2. A reliable method

items: Skim the passage once to get the general idea (topic, writer's view, how it ends).
Read each question carefully and underline the keywords.
Go back to the passage and find the sentence that answers the question.
Eliminate the options that contradict the text or add information the text never gives.
Choose the option that matches the text most closely, even if another option sounds more sensible.

blocks.x: The answer is always in the passage. Never choose an option because it is true in real life; choose it because the passage says or clearly suggests it.
3. Paraphrase and summary
To **paraphrase** is to say the same thing in different words. To **summarize** is to give the main idea in fewer words. In both cases the meaning must stay the same.

head: Statement
Good paraphrase
Why other options fail
rows: The manager was reluctant to approve the proposal.
The manager was unwilling to approve the proposal.
The chairman called off the meeting.
Although the road was damaged, the drivers continued.
The drivers continued despite the poor road.

blocks.x: 4. Linking words are clues

Words such as **although, however, despite, because, so, therefore** show how ideas connect. Contrast words (although, but, however, despite) tell you that two ideas oppose each other; cause words (because, since, as) tell you the reason; result words (so, therefore, thus) tell you the effect.
5. Worked examples

blocks.q: Choose the option that best summarizes: 'Because the market became overcrowded, the traders agreed to organize their goods in a more orderly manner.'
steps: Find the cause: the market became overcrowded.
Find the result: the traders organized their goods better.
The summary must keep the cause-and-effect link.
blocks.ans: The overcrowded market led the traders to arrange their goods more neatly.

blocks.q: Passage: 'The entrepreneur listened to her customers and improved her products.' What quality did she show?
steps: Find the actions: she listened and improved.
Ask what quality these actions show.
Match the quality with the options.

blocks.x: Do not choose an option just because it uses the same words as the passage. Wrong options often copy words from the text but change the meaning.
When two options look close, check the small words (all, only, never, always, some). Extreme words are often wrong because the passage rarely goes that far.

Cloze Passage.intro: A cloze question leaves a gap in a sentence or passage and asks you to choose the word that fits. It tests grammar, vocabulary and your sense of how English words go together. The right answer must fit both the meaning and the grammar of the sentence.

blocks.x: 1. What kinds of gaps appear

head: Gap type
Example
What decides the answer
rows: If he had studied, he ____ passed.
The clause pattern (third conditional → would have + past participle).
Fixed pairs: good at, afraid of, accused of.
He stayed at home ____ he was ill.
After 'kept', an adjective (clean) is needed, not an adverb.

blocks.x: 2. Step-by-step method

items: Read the whole sentence (or the sentence before and after) before looking at the options.
Decide what kind of word fits: a verb form, preposition, linking word, adjective or noun.
Look for clue words: if, by the time, since, yesterday, although, because.
Test each option by reading the full sentence with it in the gap.
Choose the option that is correct in both grammar and meaning.

blocks.x: 3. Linking words you must know

head: Idea
Words
Example
rows: He was absent because he was ill.
so, therefore, thus, as a result
He was tired, so he slept.
if, unless, provided that, as long as
Unless you work, you will fail.
He ran so that he would not be late.
when, while, before, after, as soon as
Call me as soon as you arrive.

blocks.x: 'Despite' and 'in spite of' are followed by a noun or -ing form, not by a full clause: 'Despite the rain' or 'Despite raining', but 'Although it rained'.
4. Worked examples

blocks.q: If Musa had arrived earlier, he ____ the beginning of the examination.
steps: 'If + past perfect' signals a past unreal condition.
The result clause needs would have + past participle.
Check the options: 'would not have missed' fits.

blocks.q: The student was absent ____ he was suffering from malaria.
steps: The second clause gives the reason for the absence.
A reason is introduced by 'because'.
'Although' and 'unless' do not give reasons.

blocks.x: Do not choose the word that merely sounds familiar. Read the sentence with every option in the gap and trust grammar rules, not feeling alone.
If two options seem right, one usually breaks a small rule (a wrong tense, a missing preposition, or a word that does not collocate). Look for that rule.

The Prescribed Reading Text.intro: Every JAMB English syllabus names a prescribed literary text (usually a novel). Questions on it test whether you actually read the book: its plot, characters, setting, themes, style and lessons. You cannot guess these answers, so you must study the book itself and use this note as a guide to how to study it.

blocks.x: 1. Know which text is required

JAMB announces the prescribed text in the current English syllabus. Always confirm the official title for your exam year from JAMB's syllabus or notice, and read that book itself. This note teaches you how to study any prescribed novel.
2. What to record while you read

head: Element
What to note
Typical question
rows: Beginning, rising action, climax, falling action, ending
What happened after...? What led to...?
Main and minor characters, traits, relationships, changes
Which character is described as...? What does X's action show?
Time and place; how it affects events
Where does the story take place?
Main ideas (e.g. justice, corruption, education, family, courage)
First person or third person narrator
From whose view is the story told?
Figures of speech, tone, symbolism, humour, irony
What figure of speech is used in...?
Moral messages and the author's purpose
What lesson does the story teach?

blocks.x: 3. A study routine

items: Read the whole book once for the story, without stopping for notes.
Read a second time chapter by chapter and write two or three lines of summary for each chapter.
Make a character list: name, role, qualities, key actions and who they are connected to.
List the main themes and attach one or two events from the book to each theme.
Collect examples of figures of speech, symbols and the writer's tone with their page numbers.
Practise past and topic questions; for each answer, find the chapter it comes from.

blocks.x: Learn events in order. Many questions ask what came before or after an event, or what caused it.
4. Character types to recognise

head: Term
Meaning
rows: The main character around whom the story revolves
The character or force that opposes the protagonist
A character whose qualities contrast with another's, making the other stand out
Complex and shows change or depth
Simple, with one main quality, and does not change

blocks.x: Do not rely on film adaptations or online summaries alone; they leave out details and sometimes change events. Questions are written from the book.
After each chapter, ask three questions: Who did what? Why did it happen? What does it show about the characters or the theme?

Synonyms.intro: A synonym is a word with the same or almost the same meaning as another word. In JAMB, the question gives a word in a sentence and asks which option is closest in meaning. The sentence is your best clue, because many words have more than one meaning.

blocks.x: 1. How to answer synonym questions

items: Read the whole sentence and work out what the word means in that sentence.
Think of your own word for it before reading the options.
Replace the word with each option and check that the sentence still makes sense.
Choose the option that keeps the meaning of the sentence.

blocks.x: Synonyms are about meaning in context, not about words that look alike. A word with a similar spelling is often a trap.
2. Words that often appear
3. Word-building clues

Roots and prefixes help you guess unknown words. **Bene-** means good (benefit, benevolent); **mal-** means bad (malicious, malnutrition); **anti-** means against; **pre-** means before; **post-** means after; **inter-** means between; **sub-** means under; **un-, in-, dis-** give a negative sense.
4. Worked examples

blocks.q: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in brackets: The witness was (reluctant) to speak publicly.
steps: 'Reluctant' means not eager to do something.
Replace it with each option: 'hesitant to speak publicly' keeps the meaning.
'Eager' and 'ready' are the opposite.

blocks.q: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in brackets: The police began to (investigate) the matter.
steps: To investigate is to look into something carefully to find the facts.
'Examine the matter' keeps the meaning of the sentence.

blocks.x: Do not choose a word because it is related to the topic. 'Doctor' is related to 'hospital', but it is not a synonym.
Keep a small notebook of 5 new words each day with a sentence for each one. Synonyms are learned from reading, not from lists alone.

Antonyms.intro: An antonym is a word with the opposite meaning of another word. JAMB gives a word in a sentence and asks for the opposite. The common trap is that one of the options is a synonym, which is the opposite of what you need.

blocks.x: 1. How to answer antonym questions

items: Find the meaning of the given word in the sentence.
Say its opposite in your own words.
Look for the option that matches your word.
Check that the other options are not synonyms (same meaning) of the given word.

blocks.x: Always read the instruction carefully: 'opposite in meaning' means antonym; 'nearest in meaning' means synonym. Under exam pressure many students mix them up.
2. Common antonym pairs
3. Negative prefixes
A negative prefix does not always give the opposite. 'Flammable' and 'inflammable' mean the same thing, and so do 'valuable' and 'invaluable' (very valuable). Know the meaning, not just the prefix.
4. Worked examples

blocks.q: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in brackets: The student was (obedient) throughout the examination.
steps: 'Obedient' means following rules and instructions.
The opposite is not following them: 'disobedient'.
Check that none of the other options means the same as 'obedient'.

blocks.q: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in brackets: The worker was (careless) with the equipment.
steps: 'Careless' means not paying attention to danger or detail.
The opposite is 'cautious' (careful).

blocks.x: Learn words in pairs: verbose/concise, scarce/plentiful, rigid/flexible. This makes the opposite appear in your mind as soon as you see the word.

Homonyms.intro: Homonyms are words that have the same spelling or sound but different meanings. In JAMB, you are given a sentence and asked what the word means in it. The sentence is the only reliable guide.

blocks.x: 1. Homonym, homophone and homograph

head: Term
Meaning
Example
rows: Same spelling and sound, different meaning
Same sound, different spelling and meaning
Same spelling, different meaning (sometimes different sound)
tear (/tɪə/ drop from eye) / tear (/teə/ to rip)

blocks.x: 2. Common words with more than one meaning

head: Word
Meaning 1
Meaning 2
rows: a place where money is kept
a place for trade and amusement
a small stick for making fire
a wooden stick for hitting a ball
brightness from the sun or a lamp
a strip of cloth worn around the neck
to fasten; to draw in a game

blocks.x: 3. How to answer

items: Read the whole sentence, not just the part with the word.
Ask: what is this word doing here (a thing, an action or a quality)?
Look at the neighbouring words for clues (e.g. 'river' → bank = land beside it).
Substitute the meaning into the sentence to test it.

blocks.q: In the sentence 'The farmers walked along the bank of the river', the word 'bank' means:
steps: The word is followed by 'of the river'.
The place beside a river is the raised ground at its edge.
A building for money does not fit the sentence.
blocks.ans: the raised ground beside a river

blocks.q: In the sentence 'She is content with her results', the word 'content' means:
steps: 'Content with' describes how someone feels.
It is an adjective meaning satisfied, not the noun meaning 'things inside'.

blocks.x: Choosing the most common meaning is the most frequent mistake. The question usually tests the less common meaning.
When a word has the same spelling but a different stress, such as CON-tent (noun) and con-TENT (adjective), the stress tells you the meaning.

Sentence Interpretation.intro: Sentence interpretation tests whether you understand what a sentence really means, including figurative expressions, negative structures, conditionals and emphasis. The skill is to restate the sentence in plain words and then match your version with the options.

blocks.x: 1. Method

items: Read the sentence slowly and underline the key words or the expression that is not literal.
Restate it in your own simple words.
Compare your version with the options.
Remove options that reverse, exaggerate or add to the meaning.

blocks.x: 2. Structures that change the meaning

head: Structure
Meaning
Example
rows: She is not unkind = She is rather kind.
a result that does not happen
He is too weak to lift it = He cannot lift it.
unreal past: I did not know
Had I known, I would have come = I did not know, so I did not come.
No sooner had he left than it rained.
Not a single student passed = All failed.
He hardly speaks = He speaks very little.
Despite the rain, the match went on.

blocks.x: 3. Idioms and figurative language

An idiom cannot be understood from the separate words. 'He has a lot on his plate' means he has many tasks, not that he is carrying food. If the literal meaning sounds strange in the sentence, look for the figurative meaning.
4. Worked examples

blocks.q: What does 'The explanation does not hold water' mean?
steps: 'Hold water' is an idiom.
If a container does not hold water, it fails.
An explanation that does not hold water is weak and unconvincing.
blocks.ans: The explanation is not logical or convincing.

blocks.q: Which option best expresses: 'Hardly had he arrived when the meeting began'?
steps: 'Hardly had...when' shows one event right after another.
He arrived and the meeting began almost immediately.
blocks.ans: The meeting began almost as soon as he arrived.

blocks.x: Do not choose an option just because it repeats words from the sentence. The correct option is often worded very differently.
Cover the options, write your own meaning first, and only then look at the choices. This protects you from tempting but wrong options.

Idioms and Figurative Expressions.intro: An idiom is a fixed expression whose meaning is different from the meanings of its words. Figurative expressions use words in a non-literal way to create an effect. JAMB tests both: what an idiom means, and what figure of speech a sentence uses.

blocks.x: 1. Common idioms and their meanings

head: Idiom
Meaning
rows: let the cat out of the bag
hit the nail on the head
say or do exactly the right thing
something that seems bad but turns out well
make people feel at ease at a first meeting
study or work late at night
the final problem that makes a situation unbearable
a small visible part of a much bigger problem
a costly possession that is useless

blocks.x: 2. Figures of speech

head: Figure
What it does
Example
rows: He is a lion in battle.
I've told you a million times.
the opposite of what is expected or said
a statement that seems false but contains truth
uses an associated word for the thing
The pen is mightier than the sword.
a gentler word for something unpleasant
I used to be a banker but lost interest.
a word that imitates a sound
addressing someone absent or a thing
O Death, where is thy sting?

blocks.x: 3. Method

items: Decide whether the expression is literal or figurative.
If figurative, think of the situation it describes.
Match that situation with the options.
Remove literal options.

blocks.q: Choose the option that best explains: 'The boy's excuse does not hold water.'
steps: The expression is an idiom.
It means the excuse is not convincing.
blocks.ans: It is not convincing or reasonable.

blocks.q: 'The wind howled in anger.' Which figure of speech is this?
steps: Howling and anger are not usually attributed to wind.
Giving human feeling to a non-human thing is personification.

blocks.x: Simile and metaphor are often confused. A simile always has 'like' or 'as'; a metaphor does not.
Learn idioms in sentences, not alone. Seeing 'bury the hatchet' used in a short story makes the meaning stay in your memory.

Word Classes and Their Functions.intro: Word classes (parts of speech) group words by the job they do in a sentence. The same word can belong to different classes in different sentences, so you must look at how a word is used, not how it looks.

blocks.x: 1. The main word classes

head: Class
Job
Example
rows: names a person, place, thing or idea
describes a verb, adjective or another adverb
shows relation to a noun or pronoun

blocks.x: 2. Function decides the class

A word class depends on use. In 'I went for a **run**', run is a noun; in 'I **run** daily', it is a verb. In 'a **round** table', round is an adjective; in 'He ran **round** the field', it is a preposition.
3. Pronouns

head: Type
Examples
rows: I, you, he, she, it, we, they
mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs

blocks.x: 4. Verbs and prepositions

Verbs may be **transitive** (take an object: He kicked the ball) or **intransitive** (no object: He slept). **Auxiliary** verbs help to form tenses (is, have, will); **modal** verbs show possibility, permission or necessity (can, may, must, should).
Many prepositions go with fixed words and must be learned in pairs.

head: Pair
Example
rows: I congratulated him on his success.
in time = early enough; on time = punctual

blocks.q: In the sentence 'I went for a run', the word 'run' is:
steps: Look at the word before it: 'a'.
'A' is used before a noun.
So 'run' names the activity: it is a noun.

blocks.x: Do not decide a word class from its ending alone. 'Friendly' ends in -ly but is an adjective, not an adverb.
To find a word's class, try these tests: can I put 'the' before it (noun)? Can I put 'very' before it (adjective or adverb)? Can I change its tense (verb)?

Clause and Sentence Patterns.intro: A sentence is built from words, phrases and clauses. JAMB asks you to recognise the type of clause, the structure of a sentence and its function. The key is to find the subject and verb of each clause and then ask what job each group of words is doing.

blocks.x: 1. Phrase and clause

A **phrase** is a group of words without its own subject and verb (in the morning, running fast). A **clause** has a subject and a verb. A **main (independent) clause** can stand alone; a **subordinate (dependent) clause** cannot.
2. Types of subordinate clause

head: Clause
Job
Example
rows: I wonder whether he will come.
The boy who won the race is my cousin.
tells when, where, why, how, etc.
He left because he was tired.

blocks.x: 3. Adverbial clauses

head: Type
Clue words
Example
rows: He was absent because he was ill.
He ran so fast that he won.
He studied so that he would pass.
If it rains, we will stay.
She sings as if she were a star.
She is taller than I am.

blocks.x: 4. Sentence structure

head: Type
Structure
Example
rows: two or more main clauses joined by and, but, or
one main + one or more subordinate clauses
He left because he was tired.
He knocked, but nobody answered because they were asleep.

blocks.x: 5. Sentence functions

head: Type
Purpose
Example
rows: The sun rises in the east.

blocks.q: In the sentence 'He ran so fast that he won', what type of clause is 'that he won'?
steps: It tells the result of running so fast.
A clause that tells the result is an adverbial clause of result.

blocks.x: Do not judge a clause by its first word alone. 'That' can start a noun clause, an adjective clause or an adverbial clause; the job it does decides the type.
To test a noun clause, replace it with 'it' or 'something'. To test an adjective clause, see if it describes a noun before it.

Grammar: Mood, Tense, Aspect, Number.intro: This topic covers how verbs show time (tense), the way an action is viewed (aspect), the speaker's attitude (mood) and how nouns show one or many (number). Most questions give a clue word in the sentence; your job is to spot the clue and apply the rule.

blocks.x: 1. Tense and aspect

head: Form
Pattern
Example
rows: She has been writing for an hour.
I was sleeping when you called.
She had left before I arrived.
She had been waiting for hours.
She will be writing at noon.
By Friday she will have written it.
By June she will have been working here for a year.

blocks.x: 2. Time clues

head: Clue
Tense
rows: since, for (up to now), already, yet, just

blocks.x: 3. Mood

head: Mood
Use
Example
rows: The sun rises in the east.
If I were rich...; I suggest that he be present.

blocks.x: 4. Conditionals

head: Type
Pattern
Example
rows: If you heat ice, it melts.
If it rains, we will stay.
If I were rich, I would build a hospital.
if + past perfect, would have + past participle
If he had studied, he would have passed.

blocks.x: 5. Reported speech

When the reporting verb is in the past, tenses shift back: **am/is → was**, **will → would**, **can → could**, **has → had**, **simple past → past perfect**. Time words change as well: **today → that day**, **tomorrow → the next day**, **yesterday → the day before**.
Direct: 'I live in Kano,' he said. Reported: He said that he lived in Kano. In reported questions the order is subject + verb: She asked me where I lived.
6. Number

head: Rule
Examples
rows: Nouns ending in s, x, ch, sh add -es
bus → buses; box → boxes; church → churches
Compound nouns pluralise the main noun
child → children; man → men; tooth → teeth
criterion → criteria; crisis → crises; stimulus → stimuli

blocks.q: If he had studied harder, he ____ the examination.
steps: 'If + past perfect' is a third conditional.
The result clause needs would have + past participle.

blocks.q: She asked me where I ____. (reported speech)
steps: The reporting verb 'asked' is in the past.
Present 'live' shifts back to past 'lived'.

blocks.x: In formal English, use 'were' for all subjects in unreal conditions: 'If I were you', not 'If I was you'.
Name the structure before you choose: third conditional, reported speech or future perfect. Naming it helps you recall the pattern.

Concord and Agreement.intro: Concord (agreement) means the verb must agree with its subject in number and person. Most errors happen when the real subject is hidden by other words. The strategy is always to find the true subject first.

blocks.x: 1. The basic rule

A singular subject takes a singular verb and a plural subject takes a plural verb. In the present tense, a singular subject (he, she, it, the boy) takes a verb with -s: **The boy runs. The boys run.**
2. Rules that cause the most mistakes

head: Rule
Example
rows: Phrases between subject and verb do not change it
The box of books is heavy.
As well as, together with, along with, accompanied by do not change the subject
The captain, along with his players, is ready.
Neither...nor, either...or, not only...but also: the verb agrees with the nearer subject
Neither the teachers nor the principal was present.
Each, every, everyone, nobody, either, neither are singular
Each of the boys has a prize.
One of + plural noun: the verb is singular
One of my friends is a doctor.
The number of → singular; a number of → plural
The number of applicants has increased. A number of students have left.
The news is good. Information was provided.
Subjects ending in -ics (subjects of study) are singular
Two nouns forming one idea are singular
Bread and butter is my breakfast.
There is / there are: the verb agrees with what follows
Amounts of money, time and distance are singular
Ten thousand naira is a lot.
Many a + singular noun takes a singular verb
More than one + singular noun takes a singular verb
More than one student was absent.

blocks.x: 3. Collective nouns

Words like **committee, team, class, jury, government, crew** take a singular verb when the group acts as one unit (The committee has reached a decision) and a plural verb when the members act separately (The committee were divided in their opinions).
4. Worked examples

blocks.q: Neither the teachers nor the principal ____ present at the meeting.
steps: The pair 'neither...nor' is used.
The noun nearest the verb is 'principal' (singular).
So the verb is singular: 'was'.

blocks.q: The number of students in the hall ____ increased.
steps: The subject is 'The number', which is singular.
'Of students' is only a phrase.

blocks.x: The commonest error is agreeing the verb with the noun nearest to it instead of the real subject. The only normal exception is after neither...nor and either...or.
Cross out any phrase between the subject and the verb. Then ask: is what is left singular or plural?

Degrees of Comparison and Question Tags.intro: Adjectives and adverbs have three degrees: positive, comparative and superlative. Question tags are short questions added to statements. Both topics follow fixed rules that are easy to score on once you learn the patterns.

blocks.x: 1. Degrees of comparison
Use the **comparative** for two things and the **superlative** for three or more. Short adjectives take -er/-est; long adjectives (three syllables or more, and many with two) take **more/most**.
Never double the comparison: 'more taller' and 'most easiest' are wrong.
2. Patterns to remember

head: Pattern
Example
rows: She is as tall as her sister.
He is taller than I am.
She is the best student in the class.
The harder you work, the better you become.
She is the taller of the two.

blocks.x: 3. Question tags
A tag repeats the auxiliary verb of the statement and uses a pronoun. **A positive statement takes a negative tag, and a negative statement takes a positive tag.**
Words such as nobody, nothing, never, hardly, scarcely, seldom and rarely have a negative meaning, so the tag is positive.

blocks.q: Complete: She hardly speaks, ____?
steps: 'Hardly' makes the statement negative.
A negative statement takes a positive tag.
The auxiliary for 'speaks' is 'does'.

blocks.q: She is the ____ of the two sisters. (tall)
steps: Two sisters are compared, so use the comparative.
With 'of the two', we say 'the taller'.

blocks.x: Do not use the superlative for two things. 'The tallest of the two' is wrong; use 'the taller of the two'.
For tags: find the auxiliary, flip positive/negative, and use the correct pronoun. With no auxiliary, use do/does/did.

Punctuation and Spelling.intro: Punctuation marks show how a sentence is built, and correct spelling shows care. JAMB tests both with short questions. The way to score is to know what job each mark does and to learn the commonly misspelt words with memory aids.

blocks.x: 1. Punctuation marks and their jobs

head: Mark
Main uses
Example
rows: ends a statement; marks an abbreviation
separates items in a list; follows an introductory word or clause; sets off extra information
Yes, I understand. He bought rice, beans and oil.
joins two closely related main clauses
She was tired; she went to bed.
introduces a list or explanation after a complete statement
You need three things: a pen, a book and a ruler.
joins words or breaks a word at a line end
adds extra information or a sudden break

blocks.x: 2. Apostrophe rules

head: Rule
Example
rows: don't = do not; it's = it is

blocks.x: Do not use a comma to join two full sentences. 'It was late, we went home' is a comma splice; use a full stop, a semicolon or a conjunction.
3. Spelling rules

head: Rule
Examples
rows: i before e, except after c
Double the final consonant after a short vowel before -ing/-ed
Change y to i before adding -es/-ed (after a consonant)
Words ending in -ful have one l

blocks.x: 4. Commonly misspelt words

head: Correct
Memory aid
rows: two m's, two t's, two e's

blocks.x: 5. Words often confused

head: Pair
Meaning
rows: principal = head or main; principle = rule
stationary = not moving; stationery = writing materials
its = belonging to it; it's = it is
their = belonging to them; there = place; they're = they are

blocks.x: Write each misspelt word correctly three times and make a memory aid. Say it in syllables: sep-a-rate, nec-es-sar-y.

Sentence Completion.intro: In sentence completion questions you choose the word or phrase that correctly finishes a sentence. These questions test grammar, vocabulary and fixed expressions, and they reward students who know common patterns.

blocks.x: 1. Method

items: Read the sentence and decide what kind of word is missing.
Look for clue words that fix a pattern (hardly, no sooner, neither, if, by the time).
Read the sentence with each option.
Choose the option that is correct in grammar and meaning.

blocks.x: 2. Fixed pairs and patterns

head: Pattern
Example
rows: Hardly had we arrived when it rained.
No sooner had he left than it rained.
Not only did he arrive late, but he also forgot his books.
Neither Ada nor Bola was present.
He was so tired that he fell asleep.
It was such a hot day that we stayed indoors.
She is too young to drive.
He is old enough to vote.
I don't know whether he will come or not.
I would rather walk than ride.

blocks.x: 3. Verb forms to watch

head: Situation
Rule
Example
rows: I look forward to seeing you.
It is time you went to bed.
I wish I had more time.

blocks.x: 4. Easily confused verbs

blocks.q: Hardly had he spoken ____ the door opened.
steps: 'Hardly' is paired with 'when'.
'Than' goes with 'no sooner'.

blocks.q: The prices have ____ sharply this year.
steps: The prices rose by themselves, so the verb has no object.
After 'have', the past participle of 'rise' is 'risen'.

blocks.x: A word can fit the meaning but break the grammar. Always test both.
Learn fixed pairs as units. When you see 'hardly', your mind should immediately supply 'when'.

Vowels.intro: Vowel questions test the sounds of English vowels, not their spellings. The same letter can represent many sounds, and the same sound can be written in many ways. To answer correctly, say each word aloud and compare the actual sound.

blocks.x: 1. The English vowel sounds
2. Spelling traps

head: Spelling
Different sounds
rows: hot /ɒ/; love /ʌ/; go /əʊ/; women /ɪ/ (the first vowel)

blocks.x: 3. How to answer

items: Say the given word and identify its vowel sound.
Say each option aloud and listen to the vowel.
Ignore the spelling and choose the option with the same sound.

blocks.q: Choose the word with the same vowel sound as the vowel in 'cup': cut, cat, cot, caught.
steps: 'Cup' has /ʌ/.
'Cut' has /ʌ/; cat has /æ/, cot /ɒ/ and caught /ɔː/.

blocks.q: Choose the word with the same vowel as in 'good': could, food, blood, flood.
steps: 'Good' has the short /ʊ/.
'Could' has /ʊ/; food has /uː/; blood and flood have /ʌ/.

blocks.x: Do not match by spelling. 'Bead' and 'head' share 'ea' but have different vowels.
Make small families: /iː/ (seat, machine, key), /uː/ (moon, rude, blue), /ɔː/ (law, sort, door). Match new words to a family.

Consonants.intro: Consonant questions test the sounds consonant letters make, which often differ from spelling. Some letters are silent, and some groups of letters (th, ch, gh, sh) have several sounds. The skill is to listen to the actual sound.

blocks.x: 1. Consonant sounds
Other consonant sounds: /m/ man, /n/ no, /ŋ/ sing, /l/ leg, /r/ red, /h/ hat, /w/ we, /j/ yes.
2. Letters with more than one sound

head: Letters
Sounds and examples
rows: /f/ laugh, enough; silent in though, night

blocks.x: 3. Silent letters
4. Endings: -ed and -s

head: Ending
Sound
Rule and examples
rows: after voiceless sounds: walked, stopped, watched
after voiced sounds: played, cleaned, begged
after /s z ʃ tʃ dʒ/: buses, wishes, churches, judges

blocks.q: Choose the word with the same consonant sound as 'th' in 'this': thin, those, bath, tooth.
steps: 'Th' in 'this' is voiced /ð/.
'Those' has /ð/; thin, bath and tooth have the voiceless /θ/.

blocks.q: Which word contains a silent letter? doubt, doctor, output, impact
steps: Say each word aloud.
In 'doubt' the 'b' is not pronounced.

blocks.x: Do not trust spelling. 'Ch' is not always /tʃ/ (machine /ʃ/, school /k/), and 'gh' is not always /f/ (laugh /f/, though silent).
Practise the voiced/voiceless pairs with your hand on your throat: voiced sounds make it vibrate.

Rhymes and Homophones.intro: Words rhyme when their endings sound the same. Homophones are words that sound the same but have different spellings and meanings. Both topics depend on sound, not spelling, so always say the words aloud.

blocks.x: 1. Rhymes
Rhyming words share the same sound from the last stressed vowel to the end: **light - fight - write**, **heart - start**, **bear - stare**, **weigh - obey**, **love - glove**, **tough - stuff**.
The -ough spelling has many sounds: bough /aʊ/, though /əʊ/, through /uː/, tough /ʌf/, cough /ɒf/, thought /ɔː/. Never rhyme by spelling.
2. Homophones

head: Word
Homophone
Meanings
rows: to put words on paper / correct; opposite of left
time of darkness / a soldier of the Middle Ages
what one / a woman with magic powers
belonging to them / in that place
to measure weight / a path or method

blocks.x: 3. How to answer

items: Say the given word and listen to its ending (for rhymes) or its whole sound (for homophones).
Say each option and compare.
For homophones, choose the word that sounds the same but is spelt differently.

blocks.q: Choose the word that rhymes with 'heart': heat, hat, hurt, start.
steps: 'Heart' is pronounced /hɑːt/.
'Start' ends with /ɑːt/.

blocks.q: Choose the word that has the same sound as 'knight' but a different spelling and meaning.
steps: 'Knight' sounds /naɪt/.
'Night' is a different word with the same sound.

blocks.x: Do not choose a word just because it looks like the given word: 'comb' and 'tomb' look alike but do not rhyme.
Learn homophones in pairs with short phrases: write a letter, turn right; see the sea; a pair of pears.

Word Stress.intro: Word stress is the extra force given to one syllable in a word. JAMB asks which syllable carries the primary stress. There are patterns that help, but you should always say the word aloud and listen for the loudest syllable.

blocks.x: 1. What stress is

Every word of two or more syllables has one **primary stress**. Stressed syllables are louder, longer and clearer. In dictionaries and in JAMB questions, the stress may be shown in capital letters: **po-li-TI-cian**, **PHO-to-graph**.
2. Patterns that help

head: Pattern
Rule
Examples
rows: REC-ord / re-CORD; PRE-sent / pre-SENT; IM-port / im-PORT
Prefix words (un-, re-, dis-) as verbs

blocks.x: 3. Stress can change the meaning or the word class
Stress also moves when a suffix is added: PHO-to-graph becomes pho-TOG-ra-phy, and E-co-no-my becomes e-co-NO-mic.
4. How to answer

items: Break the word into syllables.
Say it naturally and tap on the loudest syllable.
Check it against the patterns above.

blocks.q: In the word 'politician', on which syllable does the primary stress fall?
steps: Syllables: po-li-ti-cian.
Words ending in -cian are stressed on the syllable before the ending.
So the stress is on 'ti': po-li-TI-cian, the third syllable.

blocks.q: In the word 'photograph', on which syllable does the primary stress fall?
steps: Syllables: pho-to-graph.
It is a noun with the pattern PHO-to-graph.

blocks.x: Do not place stress by spelling or by always guessing the first syllable. Long words often carry the stress deep inside (po-li-TI-cian), but not always: A-gri-cul-ture is stressed on the first syllable. Check each word by saying it aloud.
Learn a few model words for each pattern, such as politician, economic, engineer, record, and compare new words with them.

Intonation and Emphatic Stress.intro: Intonation is the rise and fall of the voice across a sentence. It shows whether a speaker is asking, stating, doubting or finishing. Emphatic stress puts extra force on one word to show what is important or contrasted. JAMB tests which pattern fits a sentence and which word carries the emphasis.

blocks.x: 1. Basic intonation patterns

head: Pattern
Used for
Example
rows: Why did you leave? ↘  Open the door. ↘

blocks.x: 2. Common cases

head: Sentence
Normal tone
Reason
rows: Tag question when you are sure
Tag question when you do not know

blocks.x: 3. Emphatic stress
When one word is stressed more strongly than the others, it shows contrast or correction. The emphasised word answers an unstated question.

head: Sentence
What it implies
rows: I did not steal the money.
I did NOT steal the money.
I did not STEAL the money.
I did something else with it.
I did not steal THE money.
I did not steal the MONEY.

blocks.x: In 'It was YESTERDAY, not today, that he came', the stress on **yesterday** contrasts with **today**. In 'I asked for TEA, not coffee', the stress on **tea** contrasts with **coffee**.
4. How to answer

items: Decide what the speaker is doing: asking, stating, showing surprise or contrasting.
Find the word that carries the contrast, if any.
Match the tone: falling for finality and certainty, rising for questions and doubt.

blocks.q: A speaker says: 'It was YESTERDAY, not today, that he came.' Which word carries the emphatic stress?
steps: The sentence contrasts two days.
The contrasted word in capital letters is 'yesterday'.

blocks.q: Which sentence would normally end with falling intonation?  Is he your brother? / Are you coming? / Why did you leave? / Did she call?
steps: Yes/no questions rise.
Wh-questions normally fall.

blocks.x: Do not decide intonation from the question mark alone. A question mark does not always mean a rise: wh-questions normally fall.
Say the sentence aloud three times, stressing a different word each time, and notice how the meaning changes.
